w: Begun in 1248 to house relics of the Three Kings, the cathedral stalled for three centuries -- a half-built shell, a crane frozen atop one tower -- before money returned in the 1840s. Finished to the medieval plan in 1880, its facade is still the largest of any church on Earth, its spires the tallest anywhere.
s: twin spires, 632 years in the making
_facts: Construction began 1248, halted around 1560, completed to original plan in 1880
157m tall, tallest twin-spired church in the world
Largest facade of any church in the world
Houses the reliquary of the Three Kings
UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1996

w: At its core sits an oval Roman hall from the mid-4th century, its nine great cones one of the oldest sacred spaces north of the Alps. A church here was recorded by 612; archbishops added a choir around 800, before builders sheathed the whole thing in Gothic stone and raised a central dome between 1219 and 1227.
s: a Roman rotunda wearing a Gothic crown
_facts: Core is an oval Roman building from 350-365 AD
One of oldest surviving sacred buildings in Germany
First documented church on site in 612
Rebuilt into decagon with Gothic galleries and dome 1219-1227
One of the twelve Romanesque churches of Cologne

w: Raised on the ruins of a Roman cemetery, the church holds a reliquary said -- by legend -- to hold the remains of 11,000 virgins martyred alongside St. Ursula. Its Romanesque nave and tower are original; the choir was rebuilt later, Gothic. One of Cologne's twelve Romanesque churches, a minor basilica since 1920.
s: built over the bones of 11,000 virgins
_facts: Built on ruins of a Roman cemetery
Legend of 11,000 virgins martyred with St. Ursula
Reliquary made from bones of the cemetery's occupants
Nave and tower Romanesque, choir rebuilt Gothic
Minor basilica since 25 June 1920

w: Its name recalls the Roman temple to the Capitoline Triad that once stood here. Modeled on Bethlehem's Church of the Nativity and built between 1040 and 1065, it is the biggest of Cologne's twelve Romanesque churches -- 100 metres long, with a trefoil east end of three apses and three towers to the west.
s: the largest Romanesque church in Cologne
_facts: Named for Roman Capitoline Triad temple on the site
Built 1040-1065, modeled on Church of the Nativity, Bethlehem
Largest of Cologne's twelve Romanesque churches, 100m x 40m
Trefoil east end with three apses, three west towers

w: Archbishop Gero consecrated a church here in 974; it was rebuilt Romanesque in the 12th century, likely finished after the great fire of 1220. Down in the crypt, a 3rd-century Roman sarcophagus holds the bones of Albertus Magnus, the scholar-saint who taught Aquinas. Dominicans have tended it since 1947.
s: a philosopher sleeps in a Roman coffin
_facts: Consecrated 974 by Archbishop Gero
Rebuilt Romanesque in 12th century, likely finished after 1220 fire
Crypt holds Roman sarcophagus with remains of Albertus Magnus
Run by the Dominican Order since 1947

w: Before the Nazi era, Cologne had five synagogues; this Orthodox congregation on Roonstrasse is the only one still standing today. Plain from the street, it remains the anchor of Jewish life in the city -- a single survivor carrying the weight of the four that were lost.
s: the last of Cologne's five synagogues
_facts: Orthodox congregation at 50 Roonstrasse
Only surviving of Cologne's five pre-Nazi-era synagogues

w: A monastery stood here by the 10th century; the present Salian-era church rose under archbishops Heribert and Pilgrim in the early 11th, and much of its outer walls and western transept survive from that build. Like St. Maria im Kapitol, it ends in a trefoil of three apses, crowned by a 67-metre west tower.
s: Salian stonework by Cologne's busiest square
_facts: Monastery founded 10th century
Salian building begun under Archbishop Heribert (999-1021) or Pilgrim (1021-1036)
Outer walls, western transept survive from 11th century
Trefoil plan, single 67m west tower

w: Opened by chocolatier Hans Imhoff in 1993 on the Rheinauhafen peninsula, it traces chocolate from the Olmec, Maya and Aztec through to the modern factory floor visitors can watch running. Self-funded and drawing 650,000 visitors a year, it ranks among Germany's ten most-visited museums.
_facts: Opened by Hans Imhoff, 31 October 1993
Traces chocolate history from Olmec/Maya/Aztec to modern production
650,000 visitors a year, top-ten German museum
Entirely self-supporting, no subsidy

w: One of Cologne's three major museums, it holds fine art from the medieval period through the early twentieth century -- the kind of collection a smaller city would build its whole identity around. It's named for the benefactors whose bequests founded it, with a later Corboud donation folded into the title.
s: six centuries of painting in one collection
_facts: Collection spans medieval period to early 20th century
One of Cologne's three major museums
Full name includes Fondation Corboud

w: Beside the Cathedral and the Rhine, Museum Ludwig holds a modern-art collection built around Pop Art, Abstraction and Surrealism -- plus one of the largest Picasso collections anywhere in Europe, alongside stacks of Warhol and Lichtenstein.
s: one of Europe's biggest Picasso hoards
_facts: Houses Pop Art, Abstract and Surrealist works
One of the largest Picasso collections in Europe
Large holdings of Warhol and Lichtenstein

w: The museum was built over the remains of a Roman town villa so its Dionysus mosaic could stay exactly where it was found, in the basement, beside the original Roman road outside. Out front stands the old northern gate of Roman Cologne, inscribed CCAA -- the initials of the colony the whole city grew from.
_facts: Built over a Roman villa, preserving the Dionysus mosaic in place
Original Roman road preserved beside the museum
Roman northern town gate (inscribed CCAA) displayed at the front
Houses Roman glass from funerals and burials

w: A jeweller's building rented by the Nazis in 1934, turned into Cologne's Gestapo headquarters, nicknamed EL-DE Haus for its owner's initials. It survived the bombing that flattened 90 percent of the city around it. Its basement cells still carry roughly 1,800 inscriptions scratched by forced labourers and prisoners.
s: Gestapo headquarters, now the city's memory of it
_facts: Building rented by Nazis in 1934, became Gestapo HQ
Nicknamed EL-DE Haus after original owner Leopold Dahmen
Survived Allied bombing that destroyed 90% of Cologne
About 1,800 prisoner inscriptions survive in the basement cells
Won the Best in Heritage award

w: A 103-metre tower in Deutz, headquarters of the EU's aviation safety agency, with a public observation deck on its roof looking straight across the Rhine at the Cathedral's twin spires. A restaurant one floor down serves the same panorama with dinner.
s: the best view of the Cathedral is across the river
_facts: 103.2m tall, completed 2006
Headquarters of the European Aviation Safety Agency
Public observation deck on top floor
Restaurant on the floor below the deck

w: Completed in 2017 and opened by Turkish President Erdogan, this Neo-Ottoman-inspired, glass-walled complex holds up to 4,000 worshippers -- the largest mosque in Germany. Its two minarets drew local opposition before construction; today its bazaar and interfaith spaces make it as much civic landmark as place of prayer.
s: Germany's biggest mosque, minarets and all
_facts: Completed 2017, inaugurated by President Erdogan
Largest mosque in Germany, capacity 4,000
Neo-Ottoman-inspired, German Postmodern design
Includes a bazaar and interfaith spaces
